Choosing and combining models

Source: vignettes/model-choice.Rmd
model-choice.Rmd

This vignette is precomputed (dev/precompute-vignettes.R) because the Bayesian model and the backtests take several minutes.

mortensor does not have a preferred model. It implements some models directly and wraps others from established packages (demography, StMoMo, bamp, forecast), and all of them are fitted with mt_fit(), forecast with mt_forecast() and return simulated paths in the same form. They can therefore be compared in the same backtest and combined into ensembles of any composition. This vignette shows both, on one population, and leaves smoothing and the jump-off aside (see their own vignettes).

The models

Model Constructor Source Idea
Random walk with drift rwd() mortensor each log rate continues its average change; the standard benchmark of forecasting
Lee-Carter lee_carter() mortensor one time index, with an age pattern of change (Lee and Carter 1992); rotate = TRUE moves the decline to older ages as life expectancy rises (Li, Lee and Gerland 2013)
Compositional data model coda() mortensor the Lee-Carter model of the life-table distribution of deaths (Oeppen 2008; Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017)
Functional demographic model hyndman_ullah() demography rates smoothed over age, several components (Hyndman and Ullah 2007)
P-splines p_splines() mortensor a smooth surface of the log rates over age and year, extended over the forecast years (Currie, Durban and Eilers 2004)
Constrained P-splines cp_splines() mortensor the P-spline forecast, with the rates of ageing and of change of each age kept within their past range (Camarda 2019)
Rates of mortality improvement bohk_rau() mortensor a Bayesian trend of the yearly improvement of each age, from smoothed rates (Bohk-Ewald and Rau 2017)
Lee-Carter, CBD, APC, Renshaw-Haberman, M6, M7, M8, Plat stmomo("lc"), "cbd", "apc", "rh", "m6", "m7", "m8", "plat" StMoMo generalised age-period-cohort models (Cairns et al. 2009; Plat 2009; Villegas et al. 2018)
Bayesian Lee-Carter, RH, APC, CBD, M6 stanmomo("lc"), "rh", … StanMoMo the StMoMo models fitted with Stan, with posterior uncertainty of all parameters (Barigou et al. 2023)
Bayesian APC apc_bayes() bamp age, period and cohort effects with random-walk priors (Schmid and Held 2007)
Time series per age arima_series(), ets_series() forecast a separate ARIMA or exponential smoothing model for each age
Tensor decomposition tucker3() mortensor age, period and stratum factors
Several populations li_lee(), coda(coherent = TRUE), coda_causes() mortensor strata pooled around a common trend, or causes of death as shares
Coherent functional demographic model coherent_fdm() demography product-ratio method with functional data models (Hyndman, Booth and Yasmeen 2013)

The models for several populations are used in the applied vignettes; the “Model reference” lists the assumptions and the sources of uncertainty of every model.

One population, many models

Men in England & Wales, single years of age 55-90, 1971-2011 (Human Mortality Database, via StMoMo):

library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
ew <- as_mt_data(StMoMo::EWMaleData)
ew <- mt_regroup(mt_set_grid(ew, age = single_ages(55, 90, open = FALSE)), age = single_ages(55, 90, open = FALSE))
ew <- mt_subset(ew, periods = c(1971, 2011))
models <- list("random walk" = rwd(),
               "Lee-Carter" = lee_carter(),
               "fdm" = hyndman_ullah(),
               "CBD" = stmomo("cbd"),
               "APC" = stmomo("apc"),
               "M6" = stmomo("m6"),
               "M7" = stmomo("m7"),
               "Plat" = stmomo("plat"),
               "CoDa" = coda(),
               "P-splines" = p_splines(),
               "CP-splines" = cp_splines(),
               "Bohk-Rau" = bohk_rau(),
               "Bayesian APC" = apc_bayes(mcmc = mcmc_control("fast")),
               "Bayesian RH" = stanmomo("rh", h_max = 20, cores = 4))
set.seed(1)  # the MCMC samplers of bamp and Stan draw their seeds from R
fc <- lapply(models, function(m) mt_forecast(mt_fit(m, ew), h = 20, n_draws = 500, seed = 1))
#> Warning in report_fit_problems(diagnostics, spec$label, classes): Functional
#> demographic model: smooth.demogdata() failed (initial parameters not feasible);
#> smoothed without the monotonicity constraint. (diagnostics of 1 stratum/strata
#> of the fit).

The warning comes from fdm: its default smoothing over age, a spline that must increase above age 65 (demography::smooth.demogdata()), could not be fitted to these ages, so the rates were smoothed without that constraint. The same warning recurs at each backtest origin below, where it is not shown again.

Life expectancy at 55 (all models use the same ages) in 2021 and 2031:

mt_compare_forecasts(fc, periods = c(2021, 2031))
#>    label period      random walk       Lee-Carter              fdm
#> 1:  male   2021 27.4 (26.4-28.2) 27.5 (26.5-28.3) 27.7 (27.4-28.0)
#> 2:  male   2031 28.6 (27.2-29.7) 28.7 (27.5-29.8) 29.2 (28.5-29.8)
#>                 CBD              APC               M6               M7
#> 1: 27.5 (26.6-28.3) 27.4 (26.6-28.1) 27.2 (26.3-28.0) 27.5 (26.6-28.3)
#> 2: 28.7 (27.6-29.7) 28.4 (27.4-29.5) 28.1 (26.8-29.0) 28.8 (27.7-29.9)
#>                Plat             CoDa        P-splines       CP-splines
#> 1: 27.0 (26.1-27.8) 28.0 (26.2-29.1) 28.5 (27.7-29.3) 27.3 (27.1-27.5)
#> 2: 27.9 (26.6-28.9) 29.6 (28.1-30.9) 30.6 (28.3-32.1) 28.4 (28.2-28.6)
#>            Bohk-Rau     Bayesian APC      Bayesian RH
#> 1: 28.1 (27.5-28.2) 26.5 (25.5-27.4) 27.5 (26.5-28.4)
#> 2: 29.9 (29.1-30.1) 26.7 (25.0-28.2) 28.5 (27.1-29.8)
mt_plot_compare(fc[c("random walk", "Lee-Carter", "fdm", "APC", "Bayesian APC")], data = ew)

All models forecast a further rise, at different paces and with different uncertainty. By 2031 the medians range from 26.7 to 30.6 years:

  • P-splines, Bohk-Rau, CoDa and fdm give the highest forecasts (30.6, 29.9, 29.6 and 29.2 years). The P-spline surface continues the trend of each age over the last years and has the widest interval (28.3-32.1). The interval of Bohk-Rau is narrow, and its median lies close to its upper bound (29.1-30.1): the forecast improvements are limited to 3.5% a year (the upper limit of the paper), which cuts off the upper part of the distribution.
  • The period models (random walk, Lee-Carter, CBD) and M7 agree closely, at about 28.7 years.
  • The cohort models APC and M6 are lower (28.4 and 28.1 years), and Plat is lower still (27.9 years); the Bayesian RH (StanMoMo: Lee-Carter with a cohort effect, fitted with Stan) lies between them and the period models (28.5 years).
  • CP-splines forecast 28.4 years with the narrowest interval of all (28.2-28.6). Their draws carry the uncertainty of the fit only, without innovations of the trend.
  • The Bayesian APC barely moves. Its default priors are first-order random walks for period and cohort (period = "rw1"), which carry the last period effect forward without a trend; only the cohorts entering the age range change the forecast (see “Bayesian age-period-cohort models with bamp” for the alternative with second-order random walks).

The width of an interval reflects what each model treats as uncertain. Whether the medians are accurate and the intervals wide enough can only be checked against data the models did not see.

Which model forecast best

A backtest from three origins, each forecasting ten years, scores the log death rates and life expectancy at 55 (_le, in years):

bt <- mt_compare(models, ew, origins = c(1991, 1996, 2001), h = 10, n_draws = 200, quantities = "life_expectancy")
mt_score_table(bt, metrics = c("crps", "cov95"))
#>            model   crps cov95 crps_le cov95_le
#>  1:  random walk 0.0514 0.973   0.388    0.767
#>  2:   Lee-Carter 0.0571 0.688   0.365    0.933
#>  3:          fdm 0.0534 0.463   0.320    0.300
#>  4:          CBD 0.0565 0.713   0.368    0.833
#>  5:          APC 0.0393 0.947   0.261    1.000
#>  6:           M6 0.0316 0.981   0.184    1.000
#>  7:           M7 0.0523 0.816   0.374    0.800
#>  8:         Plat 0.0531 0.833   0.351    0.967
#>  9:         CoDa 0.0505 0.877   0.329    0.833
#> 10:    P-splines 0.0565 0.628   0.352    0.400
#> 11:   CP-splines 0.0624 0.359   0.497    0.100
#> 12:     Bohk-Rau 0.0337 0.682   0.108    0.867
#> 13: Bayesian APC 0.0733 0.644   0.583    0.533
#> 14:  Bayesian RH 0.0455 0.901   0.278    1.000
mt_plot_scores(bt, by = "model", target = "life_expectancy")

  • M6 forecast the rates best (CRPS 0.032), followed by Bohk-Rau (0.034) and APC (0.039). The intervals of M6 and APC covered the observed values (95% coverage of the rates 0.98 and 0.95).
  • Bohk-Rau forecast life expectancy best by far (CRPS 0.108 years, against 0.184 for M6), but its intervals are too narrow: they covered 0.68 of the observed rates and 0.87 of the observed values of life expectancy.
  • The Bayesian RH follows APC for the rates (0.0455); its 95% intervals covered 0.90 of the observed rates.
  • CoDa forecast the rates (0.0505) and life expectancy (0.329 years) less accurately than the cohort models; its intervals covered 0.88 of the rates and 0.83 of the values of life expectancy.
  • The period models and the random walk lie close together; the random walk forecast the single rates slightly better than Lee-Carter and CBD. The intervals of Lee-Carter and CBD are too narrow for the rates (95% coverage 0.69 and 0.71): their draws add only the Poisson variation of the deaths to the forecast rates. Those of the random walk, which forecasts the observed rates themselves, cover 0.97. M7, CBD with a cohort effect, forecast the rates more accurately than CBD (0.052 against 0.057), but not life expectancy. Plat forecast the rates about as accurately as M7 (0.053) and life expectancy slightly better than both (0.351 years).
  • P-splines forecast the rates about as accurately as Lee-Carter (0.0565 against 0.0571), with intervals that are too narrow (95% coverage 0.63). CP-splines were less accurate (0.062), and their intervals covered only 0.36 of the observed rates and 0.10 of the values of life expectancy.
  • fdm forecast life expectancy fairly accurately, but its intervals are far too narrow (95% coverage 0.46 for the rates and 0.30 for life expectancy).
  • The Bayesian APC is the least accurate: a forecast without a trend falls behind when mortality keeps declining.

Two cautions. Life expectancy is scored on 30 forecasts (3 origins times 10 years), so a coverage of 0.93 and one of 0.77 differ by five forecasts. And the ranking holds for this population and these years; in other data, a period model may forecast best.

Is the best model really better?

With three origins, a model can rank first by chance. mt_dm_test() tests whether the mean score of a model differs from that of a reference model by more than the origins vary (Diebold and Mariano 1995). By default the variance of the mean difference is the equal-weighted cosine estimate, with critical values from a t distribution (Lazarus, Lewis, Stock and Watson 2018), so that the test keeps its nominal size with few origins whose test years overlap. Three origins are too few: the test would have one degree of freedom. A second backtest from 16 origins (1991-2006), five years ahead, tests life expectancy at 55 against Bohk-Rau, the most accurate model for life expectancy above. To save time it leaves out fdm, CBD, M7 and the Bayesian models of bamp and Stan:

fast <- models[c("random walk", "Lee-Carter", "APC", "M6", "Plat", "CoDa", "P-splines", "CP-splines", "Bohk-Rau")]
bt_dm <- mt_compare(fast, ew, origins = 1991:2006, h = 5, n_draws = 200, quantities = "life_expectancy")
dm <- mt_dm_test(bt_dm, ref = "Bohk-Rau", targets = "life_expectancy")
dm[horizon %in% c("1", "5", "all"), list(model, horizon, df, score, score_ref, mean_diff, p_value)]
#>           model horizon df      score  score_ref    mean_diff     p_value
#>  1: random walk       1  2 0.09724537 0.09099150  0.006253872 0.157400614
#>  2: random walk       5  2 0.33916424 0.11117290  0.227991344 0.010672063
#>  3: random walk     all  2 0.20274758 0.09241699  0.110330596 0.017752259
#>  4:  Lee-Carter       1  2 0.09869128 0.09099150  0.007699773 0.029304835
#>  5:  Lee-Carter       5  2 0.33400346 0.11117290  0.222830559 0.008694245
#>  6:  Lee-Carter     all  2 0.20342037 0.09241699  0.111003388 0.017919348
#>  7:         APC       1  2 0.10308853 0.09099150  0.012097025 0.139017394
#>  8:         APC       5  2 0.22542556 0.11117290  0.114252662 0.006023920
#>  9:         APC     all  2 0.15659917 0.09241699  0.064182182 0.010681374
#> 10:          M6       1  2 0.08185772 0.09099150 -0.009133784 0.240459083
#> 11:          M6       5  2 0.18850382 0.11117290  0.077330925 0.082025317
#> 12:          M6     all  2 0.12847414 0.09241699  0.036057156 0.057652444
#> 13:        Plat       1  2 0.08671621 0.09099150 -0.004275289 0.510662864
#> 14:        Plat       5  2 0.32694266 0.11117290  0.215769759 0.008177062
#> 15:        Plat     all  2 0.19160430 0.09241699  0.099187312 0.009181521
#> 16:        CoDa       1  2 0.16356407 0.09099150  0.072572563 0.071866851
#> 17:        CoDa       5  2 0.26924964 0.11117290  0.158076743 0.003634468
#> 18:        CoDa     all  2 0.20668379 0.09241699  0.114266803 0.006512306
#> 19:   P-splines       1  2 0.13070078 0.09099150  0.039709277 0.008357861
#> 20:   P-splines       5  2 0.39054479 0.11117290  0.279371893 0.050576023
#> 21:   P-splines     all  2 0.24080913 0.09241699  0.148392140 0.051245330
#> 22:  CP-splines       1  2 0.10823133 0.09099150  0.017239831 0.041965892
#> 23:  CP-splines       5  2 0.42735305 0.11117290  0.316180154 0.006180024
#> 24:  CP-splines     all  2 0.24483804 0.09241699  0.152421054 0.017647085
#>           model horizon df      score  score_ref    mean_diff     p_value

A positive mean_diff means a higher CRPS than Bohk-Rau, so a less accurate forecast. With 16 origins the test has 2 degrees of freedom (df) and finds only large and consistent differences. Bohk-Rau had the lowest mean CRPS five years ahead and on average over the five horizons. On average, the difference is significant at the 5% level against the random walk, Lee-Carter, APC, Plat, CoDa and CP-splines (p from 0.007 to 0.018), but not against M6 (p = 0.058) and P-splines (p = 0.051). Five years ahead it is significant against the same six models (p from 0.004 to 0.011), and again not against M6 (p = 0.082) and P-splines (p = 0.051). One year ahead, M6 and Plat had a lower mean CRPS than Bohk-Rau (p = 0.24 and 0.51), and the difference is significant only against Lee-Carter, P-splines and CP-splines (p from 0.008 to 0.042). Forecasts from neighbouring origins share test years, which the test allows for. The version of forecast::dm.test() (varestimator = "acf", with the correction of Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold 1997) is an option; with few overlapping origins it rejects too often when the models are equally accurate (see ?mt_dm_test).

Ensembles of any combination

ensemble() combines any models, implemented or wrapped. Each draw of the ensemble comes from one of the components, chosen in proportion to the weights, so the ensemble is a mixture: where the components disagree, its intervals are wider than those of each component. That is often what is needed, because the disagreement between plausible models is part of the uncertainty about the future.

Weights can be equal, set by hand, or estimated from an inner backtest on the training data only (weights = "crps": inversely proportional to the CRPS of each component; "crps_stack": the stacking weights that minimise the CRPS of the mixture), and top_k keeps the best components. CRPS weights and top_k are package-specific (see the article “Methods and sources”):

ens <- list(
  "equal: Lee-Carter, fdm, APC, M6, Bayesian APC" =
    ensemble(lc = lee_carter(), fdm = hyndman_ullah(), apc = stmomo("apc"), m6 = stmomo("m6"),
             bamp = apc_bayes(mcmc = mcmc_control("fast"))),
  "CRPS weights, best 3 of 6" =
    ensemble(rw = rwd(), lc = lee_carter(), fdm = hyndman_ullah(), cbd = stmomo("cbd"), apc = stmomo("apc"),
             m6 = stmomo("m6"), weights = "crps", top_k = 3))
fit_ens <- mt_fit(ens[[2]], ew)
round(fit_ens$weights, 2)
#>   rw   lc  fdm  cbd  apc   m6 
#> 0.27 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.35 0.38

On the data up to 2011, the inner backtest kept the random walk, APC and M6, weighted by their CRPS. The ensembles in the same backtest as the single models:

bt_ens <- mt_compare(ens, ew, origins = c(1991, 1996, 2001), h = 10, n_draws = 200, quantities = "life_expectancy")
mt_score_table(rbind(bt, bt_ens), metrics = c("crps", "cov95"))
#>                                             model   crps cov95 crps_le cov95_le
#>  1:                                   random walk 0.0514 0.973   0.388    0.767
#>  2:                                    Lee-Carter 0.0571 0.688   0.365    0.933
#>  3:                                           fdm 0.0534 0.463   0.320    0.300
#>  4:                                           CBD 0.0565 0.713   0.368    0.833
#>  5:                                           APC 0.0393 0.947   0.261    1.000
#>  6:                                            M6 0.0316 0.981   0.184    1.000
#>  7:                                            M7 0.0523 0.816   0.374    0.800
#>  8:                                          Plat 0.0531 0.833   0.351    0.967
#>  9:                                          CoDa 0.0505 0.877   0.329    0.833
#> 10:                                     P-splines 0.0565 0.628   0.352    0.400
#> 11:                                    CP-splines 0.0624 0.359   0.497    0.100
#> 12:                                      Bohk-Rau 0.0337 0.682   0.108    0.867
#> 13:                                  Bayesian APC 0.0733 0.644   0.583    0.533
#> 14:                                   Bayesian RH 0.0455 0.901   0.278    1.000
#> 15: equal: Lee-Carter, fdm, APC, M6, Bayesian APC 0.0424 0.968   0.298    1.000
#> 16:                     CRPS weights, best 3 of 6 0.0354 0.980   0.238    1.000
  • The equal-weight ensemble is more accurate than the average of its components (CRPS of the rates 0.042 against 0.051), and its intervals cover. This always holds: the CRPS is a convex function of the forecast distribution, so the CRPS of a mixture is never larger than the weighted mean of the CRPS of its components. It includes the weak Bayesian APC, which pulls it behind APC and M6.
  • The CRPS-weighted ensemble comes close to M6, the best single model for the rates (CRPS 0.035 against 0.032), without knowing beforehand which model that would be: its weights were estimated anew at each origin from the years before it.

An ensemble rarely beats the best single model in hindsight. Its value is that it does not depend on picking that model in advance, and that its intervals include the disagreement between the models:

fc_ens <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(ens[[1]], ew), h = 20, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
mt_plot_compare(c(fc[c("Lee-Carter", "APC", "Bayesian APC")], list("equal ensemble" = fc_ens)), data = ew)

How to choose

  • Start from a few models that differ in their assumptions (period trend only, cohort effects, smooth age pattern) and a benchmark (rwd()).
  • Compare them in a backtest on the quantity the analysis is about, with the accuracy (CRPS) and the coverage of the intervals, and test whether the differences are larger than chance (mt_dm_test()); more origins make the test more sensitive.
  • Where no model is clearly best, or the single models are too narrow, use an ensemble; estimated weights (weights = "crps", top_k) are re-estimated at every backtest origin, so they can be checked in the same way.
  • For several populations (sexes, regions, deprivation groups) add the pooled models (li_lee(), coherent_fdm()) and make totals coherent (reconciled()); see the applied vignettes.
